concepts.title: List Indexing Positive and Negative
concepts.definition: Every element of a list sits at a numbered position called an index, counted from 0 at the front. Python also counts backwards: index -1 reaches the last element, -2 the one before it, and so on, so the same element has a positive and a negative address differing by the list length.
concepts.key_idea: The last element lives at count minus one going forward, and at minus one going backward; an index past either end raises IndexError.
question_patterns: what index does the last element of a 6-element list have
what negative index refers to the first element of a list
for list1 = [2,4,6,8,10,12], what do list1[3] and list1[-1] return

write an expression using len() to fetch the last element of any list
how is list1[n-1] different from list1[-n] for length n

solution_steps.explain: indices run 0 to count-1, so subtract one from the element count
the backward address equals the forward address shifted by the full count

concepts.title: List Slicing With a Step Value
concepts.definition: Slicing copies a stretch of a list as list1[start:stop:step], where the stop position is excluded. A missing start means the beginning, a missing stop means the end, and a step greater than one skips elements; a negative step even walks the list backwards.
concepts.key_idea: Count the picked elements by rounding the span upward against the step; stop is never included.
question_patterns: what does list1[0:6:2] return for the seven-colour list of the chapter
how many elements does the slice list1[2:6] contain
why does list1[7:2] give an empty list

solution_steps.action: measure the width of the cut
solution_steps.explain: the span is the stop position minus the start position

solution_steps.action: round the span up against the step
solution_steps.explain: dividing the span by the step and rounding upward counts how many elements survive the cut

concepts.title: Concatenation and Repetition Operators
concepts.definition: The + operator glues two lists end to end into a fresh list without touching the originals, and it refuses to mix a list with a non-list operand (TypeError). The * operator repeats a whole list a whole number of times, so a joined list repeated three times grows to triple its length.
concepts.key_idea: Joining adds the two lengths; repetition multiplies the length by the repeat factor; originals stay unchanged.
question_patterns: join [1,3,5,7,9] and [2,4,6,8,10] with + and state the result
how many elements does (list1 + list2) contain if list1 has 5 and list2 has 5 elements

solution_steps.explain: concatenation lines the second list up behind the first, so lengths simply add
repetition copies the joined list, multiplying its length by the repeat count

concepts.title: Built-in Functions on Lists: sum, min, max
concepts.definition: Python ships ready-made helpers for numeric lists: sum() totals the elements, min() and max() report the smallest and largest, and dividing the total by the element count gives the mean. These functions read the list but never alter it.
concepts.key_idea: Total the marks, then divide by how many students there are; the smallest and largest come straight from min and max.

concepts.title: List Methods: append, extend, insert
concepts.definition: Growing methods differ in what counts as one addition: append() puts a single item at the end, even if that item is itself a whole list nested as one element; extend() unpacks its argument and appends each element separately; insert(pos, item) slots an item at a chosen position and pushes the rest sideways.
concepts.key_idea: append grows the list by exactly one no matter what it adds, extend grows it by the argument's length.
concepts.textbook_ref: keip104.txt Table 4.1 append/extend/insert rows and Exercise Q2 (lines 300-331, 1067-1074)
question_patterns: differentiate between append() and extend() with the list [10,20,30,40]

solution_steps.explain: append adds exactly one item, even a nested list, so the count rises by 1

solution_steps.action: grow by the argument size for extend
solution_steps.explain: extend unpacks the incoming list, adding as many elements as it holds

concepts.title: Traversing a List with a Loop
concepts.definition: Walking through a list one element at a time is called traversal. A for loop can visit the elements directly, or pair range() with len() to visit them by position; a while loop does the same with a manual counter that must be advanced each round.
concepts.key_idea: for item in list1 gives values, while range(len(list1)) gives positions you can also overwrite.

solution_steps.action: pick the direct or index style
solution_steps.explain: for item in list1 yields values; for i in range(len(list1)) yields positions

solution_steps.action: apply any test inside the loop body
solution_steps.explain: an if inside the loop filters, for example keeping only even indices

solution_steps.action: confirm the loop ends when elements run out
solution_steps.explain: the for loop stops automatically once every element has been visited

concepts.title: Dictionary Keys, Values and Membership
concepts.definition: A dictionary stores items as key-value pairs inside curly braces, each key joined to its value by a colon. Keys must be unique and immutable and work like labels; a missing key raises KeyError, while the in operator checks whether a key exists without fetching anything.
concepts.key_idea: Keys are looked up, not positions: the same key always maps to the same value wherever the item sits.

solution_steps.explain: dictionary items are reached by key in square brackets, never by position
an existing key returns its value; an unknown key raises KeyError, or get() returns None

solution_steps.action: use membership for a safe test
solution_steps.explain: key in dict answers True or False before any lookup is attempted

worked_examples.q: Fetching a missing key directly raises which error?

concepts.title: Dictionary Methods: len, update, del
concepts.definition: Dictionary upkeep uses len() to count pairs, update() to merge another dictionary's pairs in, get() to fetch a value or None for a missing key, and del to remove one pair by key or the whole dictionary from memory. Merging first and deleting later leaves a size that can be tracked arithmetically.
concepts.key_idea: Each merged pair raises the pair count by one; each deleted key lowers it by one; len() always reports the current total.
question_patterns: after dict1.update({'Sohan':79,'Geeta':89}) on a 4-pair dictionary, what does len(dict1) return

solution_steps.explain: update() appends each incoming key-value pair, so the pair count grows by the incoming number
each del of one key removes exactly one pair from the total
